title: Stine-Morrow (2007): Discussion Preparation
instructions: Practice a 30-second response: state your conclusion, give evidence from the article, and add a precise conceptual distinction, limitation, or family and education application. Identify applications as your own inferences.

cards.title: State the article's central argument in one sentence.
cards.answer_30s: Cognitive aging may depend partly on choices about allocating effort, alongside genetically driven senescence and accumulated abilities. Choices may act directly through attentional engagement in a current task and indirectly as experience shapes the neural foundations of component abilities. Stine-Morrow advances this as an argument to investigate, rather than an established causal law.

cards.title: Distinguish mental mechanics from cultural and pragmatic competence.
cards.answer_30s: Mental mechanics are fluid abilities involved in rapidly encoding and transforming new information, which normally tend to decline with age. Crystallized abilities depend on knowledge and the acquisition of culture, and may remain stable or increase well into later life. Cognitive aging therefore involves more than uniform decline. The article adds choices about effort allocation to this account of competing developmental forces.

cards.title: How does attentional engagement differ from activity engagement?
cards.answer_30s: Attentional engagement means allocating resources to the cognitive processes needed for a selected task, supporting current performance. Activity engagement means habitually choosing intellectually stimulating environments that may shape or expand capacity over time. The distinction is between how we process a task and which environments and activities we choose to enter.

cards.title: Explain the negative feedback loops in the SRLP model.
cards.answer_30s: At the surface-form, textbase, and situation-model levels, readers compare their perceived understanding with a reference value. If understanding is not good enough, the relevant processor requests more resources until perceived comprehension meets the criterion. Negative feedback means regulation that reduces a discrepancy, rather than a harmful effect. The reference values are influenced by readers' cognitive and socioemotional goals.

cards.title: What is allocation policy, and how is it measured?
cards.answer_30s: Allocation policy describes how readers adjust reading time as text-processing demands vary. Regression coefficients capture relative changes in reading time, such as extra time for words introducing new concepts or for integration at clause and sentence endings. The measure characterizes responsiveness to particular text demands, rather than simply whether someone reads slowly overall.

cards.title: What age difference appeared in the study of accuracy goals?
cards.answer_30s: Participants read short texts either for accurate recall or to get the main idea efficiently. Younger readers were especially responsive to the accuracy goal, increasing reading time as informational density rose. Older readers responded less to the stricter criterion for information acquisition. Working-memory capacity and memory self-efficacy each accounted for part of the age difference in responsiveness.

cards.title: How do the memory self-efficacy findings differ from an explanation based only on limited ability?
cards.answer_30s: Memory self-efficacy concerns beliefs that one's effort can affect memory performance. Along with working-memory capacity, it explained part of the age difference in responding to an accuracy goal. Older readers' reluctance therefore cannot be interpreted only as inability. The author also describes unpublished evidence that specific instructions on conceptual integration can induce more thorough semantic analysis, distinguishing available capacity from willingness to recruit resources.

cards.title: Why does the association between an active lifestyle and better cognition fall short of causal evidence?
cards.answer_30s: People in intellectually challenging environments may live longer and score better cognitively, but those with greater initial vitality may be more likely to select and remain in such environments. Occupational engagement, leisure activity, and vulnerability to dementia might also reflect a common genetically driven aging process. These observational associations do not establish that activity itself prevented cognitive decline.

cards.title: Distinguish selection effects from a common-cause explanation.
cards.answer_30s: A selection explanation emphasizes that people with greater initial vitality are more likely to enter intellectual activities and sustain participation. A common-cause explanation treats activity, cognitive performance, and dementia vulnerability as possible biobehavioral indicators of the same underlying aging process. Both limit causal inference, but one emphasizes selection into participation and the other a shared underlying cause.

cards.title: What role does cognitive reserve play in the argument?
cards.answer_30s: The article describes evidence that lower education is an Alzheimer's disease risk factor and that more highly educated people can tolerate pathology longer before showing clinical symptoms. These findings are harder to explain through selection alone. Cognitive reserve proposes that rich experience strengthens neural circuitry and alternative repertoires for functioning despite pathology. The article does not newly establish a direct causal effect of education.

cards.title: Describe the design and central findings of the ACTIVE trial.
cards.answer_30s: ACTIVE was a randomized clinical trial that gave older adults 10 sessions of training in memory, processing speed, or reasoning and compared them with a no-contact control group. Training effects were retained for up to five years. The benefits were highly specific: speed training improved speeded tasks but did not transfer to memory or reasoning.

cards.title: What exactly does the article report about transfer from ACTIVE to everyday activities?
cards.answer_30s: The article states that transfer to everyday analogues of the trained abilities had not been demonstrated. Participants who received reasoning training did report greater ease with instrumental activities of daily living, such as preparing meals or paying bills. Self-reported ease and demonstrated transfer to everyday performance therefore need to remain distinct conclusions.

cards.title: Why does the author compare engagement with education rather than training?
cards.answer_30s: Training and expertise studies suggest that experience often benefits the specific abilities practiced. Training prepares a defined set of skills, whereas education prepares people to act in unpredictable contexts. Activity engagement requires choices about selecting, prioritizing, and structuring unfamiliar problems and organizing resources. Drawing on skills as needed might produce broader effects, but that pathway was still largely unexplored.

cards.title: Describe the features and findings of Senior Odyssey.
cards.answer_30s: Senior Odyssey combined collaborative, ill-defined long-term problems, quick spontaneous challenges, creativity, friendly competition, activity choices, and age integration. Preliminary findings showed better processing speed and marginal improvement in divergent thinking relative to wait-list controls, alongside relative increases in mindfulness and need for cognition. Whether the program produced broad improvements in cognitive functioning remained an open hypothesis.

cards.title: What might you propose when applying the article to family or educational settings?
cards.answer_30s: My application would be to offer older adults choices among meaningful, emotionally satisfying intellectual challenges and opportunities to attend to the skills those challenges require. Families and educators need not assume that capacity is entirely fixed. This is an inference from the argument, not a tested family intervention. Supporting choice, novelty, and self-regulation should not become a promise that participation will prevent decline.

reading_response.title: Reading Response: How Did You Read the Article?
reading_response.instructions: Use your own words to connect what was new, how your view changed, specific evidence, and limitations. Keep your claims within the article's evidence and identify personal applications as inferences.

cards.title: Give your basic 30-second response to the article.
cards.answer_30s: I read this as a proposal that effort allocation and choices of intellectual environments may provide additional routes to cognitive vitality while senescence and capacity constraints still matter. It is not a claim that willpower alone determines performance. The interaction between attentional engagement in selected tasks and habitual activity engagement still requires empirical examination.

cards.title: What finding stood out most to you?
cards.answer_30s: The finding that younger readers adjusted their reading time more strongly than older readers when accurate recall was required stood out to me. Working memory explained part of the difference, but so did beliefs about being able to influence memory outcomes. I found it useful to distinguish available capacity from beliefs that may affect whether people recruit their resources.

cards.title: How did the article change your previous understanding?
cards.answer_30s: I had tended to interpret better cognition among intellectually active people as evidence that activity was protective. The article separates the possibility that initially more vital people select and sustain participation from the possibility that several indicators share an underlying aging process. I now look for selection effects and common causes before interpreting an observational association causally.

cards.title: How did ACTIVE change the way you think about brain training?
cards.answer_30s: I now ask what was trained and where benefits transferred, rather than asking only whether training works. In ACTIVE, effects of 10 training sessions persisted for up to five years, but speed-training benefits did not extend to memory or reasoning, and everyday transfer had not been demonstrated. I would distinguish improvement in a specific ability from broad cognitive vitality.

cards.title: What question or limitation remained for you?
cards.answer_30s: Senior Odyssey showed preliminary changes in processing speed and engagement-related dispositions, but broad cognitive improvement remained unestablished. I would like to know which components of an intervention resembling everyday life matter, and whether benefits extend to untrained abilities and everyday performance. I read the results within the stated context of ongoing program development and evaluation.

cards.title: How would you connect the article to family life?
cards.answer_30s: My application would be for families to support older adults in choosing meaningful new activities and giving the necessary processes sufficient attention, rather than treating a slower response as proof of inability. This is my interpretation of the article's self-regulation perspective. The article does not directly establish that a particular form of family support prevents cognitive decline.
